Chapter 3: The ‘Between Times’ — Why Adoption Lags Behind Technology
Let’s dive into a challenge that doesn’t get talked about enough. Even though AI is bursting with promise, the journey from a shiny new breakthrough to something everybody uses isn’t instant. In fact, there’s this awkward middle phase—people sometimes call it the ‘between times.’ It can last for years, even decades. The technology is there, but organizations just aren’t set up to take full advantage of it yet. So, progress is a bit messy—full of stops, starts, and lots of trial and error.
Why does it happen this way? Well, think of technology as just one piece of a much bigger puzzle. For AI to really shine, it needs to be woven into company processes, structures, and—maybe the hardest part—company culture. And as you probably know, those things don’t change overnight. This is especially true with prediction technologies, since they touch so many parts of an organization and often mean folks need to work in totally new ways.
So, what holds AI adoption back? There are a few big hurdles:
First, organizational inertia. Companies have routines, hierarchies, and sometimes a lot of people who feel threatened by change—especially if it might impact their roles or influence.
Next, there’s the need for complementary investments. AI isn’t just plug-and-play. It often demands new data systems, training, and a shake-up in how work gets done. All of that can be expensive and risky, particularly if it’s not clear yet what the payoff will be.
Then, regulatory and ethical concerns come into play. Think about using AI in healthcare, banking, or the justice system—suddenly, questions about fairness, accountability, and transparency become huge. Navigating those issues can really slow things down.
Finally, there’s just a lot of uncertainty about value. Sometimes, organizations aren’t quite sure how to use AI, or even what new opportunities it could open up. So, they might run a few pilot projects, but hesitate to really commit until they see solid results.
Here’s a great real-world example: the early days of electrification. When electricity first came to factories, most managers just swapped out steam engines for electric motors and left everything else the same. It took decades before folks realized electricity could transform the whole way factories worked—with things like assembly lines and flexible workstations. The biggest gains came not from just updating the tech, but by completely rethinking what was possible.
We’re seeing that same story replay with AI. At first, companies use AI for pretty simple stuff—like sorting resumes or spotting fraud. Sure, that’s helpful, but it’s just scratching the surface. The real magic happens when organizations redesign how they work to really play to AI’s strengths—using real-time data to tailor services or creating products no one imagined before.
Honestly, this in-between period can be frustrating. The technology’s ready, but the big benefits take time to show up. Some organizations are bold—they experiment, make mistakes, and learn as they go. Others hang back, worried about risks and unknowns. But as more companies figure out what works, and the value of AI becomes clearer, adoption picks up speed. Eventually, these ‘between times’ fade, and AI becomes just part of how things get done.
Here’s something important to remember: this isn’t just a technical challenge—it’s a human one. It takes new mindsets, building trust, and managing the push and pull of different interests and incentives. Technology matters, but so does the ability to lead change, bring people together, and learn from experience.
So, the big takeaway here? The road from AI breakthroughs to real-world impact is shaped by the slow, sometimes messy work of adapting organizations and institutions. These ‘between times’ are a necessary part of the journey—helping us figure out how to truly harness the power of prediction and weave it into our everyday lives.
